projects.title: Arista Networks (ANET) stock pitch
projects.org: Equity research pitch · prepared with Perplexity
projects.question: Is Arista Networks the best way to own AI data-center networking spend?
projects.theory: Equity research: investment thesis, scenario DCF, peer comparison and risk framing.
bullets: Recommended Strong Buy with a $175 12-month target (+30.9% from $133.64) and a $115 stop loss
Built a three-scenario DCF (base case $155) and compared Arista with NVIDIA and Cisco on growth, margins, balance sheet and valuation
Defined entry and exit triggers, the main risks (42% of revenue from Microsoft and Meta) and a falsifiable catalyst to track
projects.note: Research exercise using data as of Apr 7, 2026. Not investment advice.
overview: A 12-month investment pitch recommending Arista Networks as a way to own AI data-center networking spend. The thesis rests on Arista's position in AI Ethernet networking, its EOS software and the upgrade cycle from 800G to 1.6T networking.

I tested it with a three-scenario DCF (bear $70, base $155, bull $215), a comparison with NVIDIA and Cisco, entry and exit triggers, and a risk section naming customer concentration (Microsoft and Meta, 42% of revenue) as the main threat. The pitch also states a falsifiable claim: if no fourth 10%+ customer is announced by Q4 2026 earnings, the target falls to $145.
Prices and data are as of April 7, 2026, and the memo was prepared with Perplexity. It is a research exercise, not investment advice.

projects.title: Beverage industry equity research: Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, Monster, Celsius, Keurig Dr Pepper
projects.org: Brandeis coursework · group project of five
projects.question: How should a moderately risk-averse investor allocate across five U.S. beverage companies?
projects.theory: Financial ratio analysis, cost of capital (CAPM and WACC) and payout policy.
bullets: Compared the five companies over 2021–2025 on liquidity, solvency, asset management, profitability and market value ratios
Estimated beta, cost of equity, cost of debt and WACC for each company and benchmarked them against a 6.33% industry WACC
Analyzed dividend and buyback policy to separate income-focused from growth-focused companies
results: WACC ranged from 6.72% (PepsiCo) to 13.75% (Celsius), with beta the main driver
Recommended a 40% PepsiCo, 40% Coca-Cola and 20% Monster portfolio, excluding Keurig Dr Pepper and Celsius
overview: A comparative study of Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, Monster Beverage, Celsius and Keurig Dr Pepper from 2021 to 2025, completed as a group of five. Part I compared the companies on liquidity, solvency, asset management, profitability and market value ratios.

Part II estimated each company's cost of capital using CAPM, with bond yields or synthetic ratings for the cost of debt, and compared the results with a 6.33% industry WACC. It also reviewed dividend and buyback policy.

The conclusion was a 40% PepsiCo, 40% Coca-Cola and 20% Monster allocation for a moderately risk-averse investor. Keurig Dr Pepper (higher beta and leverage, thinner interest coverage) and Celsius (beta of 1.81 and a 13.75% WACC) were excluded.

projects.title: Corporate financial model: Church & Dwight (NYSE: CHD)
projects.question: What is Church & Dwight worth, and what drives its forecast?
projects.theory: Three-statement integration, scenario analysis, WACC and discounted cash flow (DCF) valuation.
bullets: Built an integrated financial model with base, best and worst case scenarios and a five-year forecast (2026–2030)
Estimated a 7.26% WACC from a CAPM cost of equity of 7.74% and a 4.19% weighted cost of debt, with 3% terminal growth
Valued the company with a DCF and cross-checked it with P/E, EBITDA and revenue multiples and a WACC and growth sensitivity table
results: Base case DCF value of $100.10 per share against a $92.65 market price; probability-weighted value of $105.76
overview: Built for the Corporate Financial Modeling course. The workbook links an assumptions table to an integrated financial model, three scenarios (base 50%, best 25%, worst 25%), a WACC model built from the company's debt structure and a CAPM cost of equity, a DCF and a multiples valuation.
The base case values the stock at $100.10 per share against a $92.65 market price. Weighting the scenarios gives $105.76, and the model recommends HOLD.

projects.title: Python stock portfolio analyzer: Big Tech vs the S&P 500
projects.question: Did an equal-weight Big Tech portfolio beat the S&P 500 once risk is taken into account?
projects.theory: Portfolio construction and risk-adjusted performance: volatility, Sharpe ratio and maximum drawdown.
bullets: Downloaded and cleaned 2025 prices for Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Tesla and the S&P 500
Built an equal-weight $10,000 portfolio and tracked its daily value against the index
Calculated total and annualized return, volatility, Sharpe ratio and maximum drawdown, and charted every stock, the portfolio and the index
results: The portfolio returned 23.5% against 16.7% for the S&P 500, growing $10,000 to $12,353
It took more risk: volatility of 28.8% against 18.8% and a maximum drawdown of −29.3% against −18.9%, so the Sharpe ratios were almost equal (0.81 vs 0.82)
Alphabet contributed the most (+65.9%) and Tesla was the most volatile stock
overview: Framed as a client request: evaluate an equal-weight $10,000 investment in Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Tesla, and benchmark it against the S&P 500 for 2025.

The notebook downloads and cleans the price data, builds the portfolio, charts every stock against the index, and calculates return, volatility, Sharpe ratio and maximum drawdown. The portfolio beat the index on return (23.5% vs 16.7%) but with more volatility and deeper drawdowns, so on a risk-adjusted basis it was roughly level with the S&P 500 (Sharpe ratio 0.81 vs 0.82).
